offence_severity: Minimum: Life imprisonment, Maximum: Life imprisonment
physical_harm: Multiple stab injuries leading to the victim's death three days later
number_of_offences: Number of offences/counts charged: 8, Number finally upheld: 7
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation/planning due to previous animosity and the use of weapons
key_evidence_accepted: The court accepted the testimony of the eye-witnesses PW2 and PW3, the dying declaration of the victim, and the presence of the witnesses at the place of occurrence.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, noting that their testimony was detailed and not based on mere chance, despite the lack of electricity at the scene.
trial_duration: Offence: 14.05.1996; Trial judgment: 22.03.2007; High Court decision: 22.03.2007; Supreme Court decision: 24.04.2015
legal_representation: Nagendra Rai, A.T.M. Rangaramanujam, P. N. Ramalingam for the Appellant; June Chaudhary, D. Mahesh Babu, Amit K. Nair, T. V. Bhaskar Reddy, Amjid Maqbool for the Respondent
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction; High Court: Acquittal of A4, A8 and A9, conviction of others upheld; Supreme Court: Upheld High Court decision
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused were part of an unlawful assembly armed with weapons, and that the dying declaration of the victim was reliable. They also contended that the presence of the accused at the scene of the crime was established, and that the plea of alibi was not credible. The prosecution further maintained that the nature of injuries and previous animosity indicated intent to kill, and that the offense under Section 302 IPC should not be converted to Section 304 Part I IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution witnesses were 'chance witnesses' and their testimony was unreliable. They also contended that the dying declaration was vague and not specific enough to attribute specific acts to the accused. The defence further claimed that the accused were falsely implicated and that the absence of a charge under Section 149 IPC was a fundamental defect that warranted acquittal.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the absence of a charge under Section 149 IPC is not per se fatal, and that the burden of proof lies with the accused to establish their alibi with certainty. The Court also emphasized that the reliability of the dying declaration is crucial for conviction.
precedent_relied_upon: Willie (William) Slaney v. State of M.P., Annareddy Sambasiva Reddy v. State of A.P., Rana Pratap D and others v. State of Haryana, Jarnail Singh v. State of Punjab, Mehiboobsab Abbasabi Nadaf v. State of Kamataka, Kashi Vishwanath v. State of Kamataka, Binay Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar, Gurpreet Singh v. State of Haryana, S.K. Sattar v. State of Maharashtra, Jitender Kumar v. State of Haryana
